utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Lieutenant, I know you may remember, but it is my job to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Poje. We are going to continue where we left off yesterday and we were discussing the expert report of yours. We reached chapter 3.5 which is titled "artillery ammunition," page 17 of the B/C/S or page 13 of the English. When you talk about artillery ammunition, you stress in the first paragraph underneath the heading that the important thing is that in the weapons system there is a projectile which has to be launched at a target at a certain distance for the purpose of carrying out a task. When you say that, you are speaking generally, are you not, and dealing with the situation when you use conventional artillery and when you're using a multiple-barrelled rocket launcher. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In fact, I'm talking about a projectile which was either launched with a gunpowder charge from the conventional artillery barrel or a projectile which has its own in-built motor, that is to say a rocket system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, you go on to explain in that same chapter that this projectile with propulsion elements and guidance and stabilisation and with effects on the target is an -- is a form of ammunition for one system of weapons relating -- and that also relates to the Orkan M87 multiple-barrelled rocket launcher, does it not, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you deal with the topic of artillery ammunition further on in the chapter, you say that as opposed to the other systems and elements in the weapons system, ammunition represents an energetic system, the effects of which are short. And I assume -- short-lived effect, single-use energy devices with a short-lived effect. So I assume you refer to a charge, a motor, and the explosive that if -- hits the target. Is that right, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The projectile that I looked at, you have this motor section that puts the projectile into motion, that's one group, propulsion; and the other with the gunpowder charge that is activated upon impact. So what you said is roughly correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in that same chapter entitled "artillery ammunition," under point 3.5.1, the title there is "conventional projectiles." And in that paragraph you say that regardless of the type and calibre of the type of artillery weapon, an artillery shell has the following constituent parts: A projectile, a gunpowder charge, cartridge, and primer. Now, when you say that, you're referring to conventional artillery, are you not, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, for the most part. All types of projectiles with -- and all the ammunition were just dealing with the energy propulsion by the projectile, because it is separately packaged into little bags or it can be a component part of the projectile itself, as is the case with rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, further on you go on to say that the projectile is the most important element of a shell, as it produces an effect on the target with its bursting charge and jacket fragments. Now, in that respect, the question is: Do the bomblets that we saw yesterday, an example of the bomblet, is that a projectile of an artillery rocket of the Orkan type?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The projectile in this case is the rocket itself with its cluster warhead, whereas the bomblets are just one of the elements of a cluster warhead, which instead of the cluster acts on the target or the explosive charge in convention [as interpreted] artillery. So it's not the rocket that targets, it is its individual parts to be found in the cluster warhead that have the destructive effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I feel that it is necessary to stress at this point, as a general characteristic of artillery ammunition and artillery projectiles or shells, is what you say here in fact, that an artillery projectile affects the target with its bursting charge and jacket fragments. Now, the question is: Is that what every artillery projectile does, including Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle this is how it works with conventional projectiles where the cluster war -- where the warhead -- in a classical projectile the warhead hits the target or obstacle upon impact. The fuse is ignited, there is initial charge which is activated, and in conventional weapons it is this warhead which impacts on the target itself. But with the Orkan rocket system the warhead, the cluster warhead is activated at an altitude of approximately 800 metres. It opens up in a very specific way and ejects from that warhead 288 bomblets. And in fact, what affects the target is not the warhead of the rocket itself but it is these bomblets which are to be found in the cluster warhead itself and which then fall freely after the cluster warhead opens, fall towards the target or obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to understand the term "projectile" or "artillery projectile," it would be a good idea to look at the diagram on page 22 of the B/C/S text and page 18 of the English text. And this diagram is -- represents a rocket projectile with high explosive -- with a high explosive warhead. Now, can we say that this schematic, this diagram, in principle, is what an artillery projectile looks like in general terms, whether it is a conventional weapon or if we're dealing with the multiple-barrelled rocket launcher. That is the shape of an artillery shell. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this diagram in fact shows a projectile, we can say, of the conventional type, a conventional projectile, with a warhead and with the fragmentation effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that point 1, under 1, in this diagram we have the fuse?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that that fuse, when the projectile impacts the target, activates the warhead and brings about the explosion or what the projectile is supposed to do, explode?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, the primer, the fuse, can be a delayed-fire fuse. In the first case it activates the warhead upon impact; in the second example, if we're dealing with a tank fuse, there's an explosion which is delayed, an explosion along the trajectory itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje. Now, with respect to the type of fuses, the primers, the delayed-fire action, and so on and so forth, we'll deal with that later on, but I'd just like to dwell on a diagram. This diagram, number 4, is explosive charge, and that is the top part of the projectile with the dotted area. Now, I want to ask you this: In principle does every artillery projectile in its first part, whether it is a conventional shell or a rocket projectile, has this explosive charge? Are the explosive charges the same in the initial part of the projectile?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the conventional type of fuge projectile, then every projectile or its warhead does have this type of explosive charge, which is shown under number 4 of the diagram, and it is the dark line, the shaded part of the warhead. What we see here, however, does not relate to the Orkan rocket system because you can't see a cluster warhead here. This is just a conventional warhead which, according to the design of the projectile, has a different effect than does a cluster warhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to that last answer of yours, instead of point 4 here, the dotted, shaded area, with Orkan we have the cluster warhead which is composed of the 288 bomblets that we saw instead of this explosive charge. And then those bomblets at a certain altitude above the target disperse because the rocket opens -- its outer layer opens up?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So in a cluster warhead, instead of the explosive charge shown under number 4 on this diagram, what we have is the 288 bomblets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And since we're dealing with this diagram, if you look at number 7 there's a dark grey area and that comes below this explosive charge and that would be the rocket powder or the energy propulsing [as interpreted] the rocket?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the fuel, if you like to call it, or the energy that gives energy to the projectile, sets it off on its trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that the Orkan rocket system is, in fact, a conventional artillery projectile whose explosive charge has a cluster shape or, rather, is -- consists of 288 bomblets?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Orkan rocket is a classical or conventional projectile, but the difference is that instead of having just a conventional warhead it has a cluster warhead which contains the 288 bomblets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, under point 3.5.2, page 20 -- that is to say we go back two pages. Chapter, point -- 3.5.2 is entitled "rocket projectiles." And in that chapter you are, in fact, saying what you told me a moment ago: A rocket projectile has all the properties of ammunition and that one of its properties is that it is launched from a launcher instead of a gun barrel and that these can either be tubes or tracks?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The difference between a conventional system, a Howitzer system, a gun Howitzer system, these conventional weapons is that the projectiles are ejected from barrels or tubes in a specific way, based on the charge placed in the gunpowder section, whereas the rocket systems launch their projectiles, which means that the projectile which is being launched contains a rocket motor which supplies the kinetic energy to them. And so the rocket projectiles have an energy group or charge group, which propels them, whereas classical or conventional ammunition most frequently do not have this part which is separate, this charge part separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, further on in the text, when you mention the Orkan system you say that regardless of the difference in the type of launching, an artillery projectile, for example with guns projected -- ejected from a tube or barrel, whereas the rocket launcher launches this from tubes or tracks. So regardless of this difference you say that the trajectory of a multiple rocket launcher projectile is set in advance, and to all intents and purposes is no different from the conventional projectiles. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, precisely. Because the elements for launching are determined beforehand, depending on the position, the position of the target, meteorological and ballistic conditions, firing, the elements for firing are calculated, and then these positions are adjusted on the launcher. There is a time-fuse on the projectile itself, and it is these elements which launch the rocket towards its target, or projectile towards its target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the continuation of the text you tell us how the rocket flies to its target, and you state that the basic difference between a conventional projectile and a rocket projectile lies in the fact that a rocket projectile has its own built-in flight projectile control electronic systems and motor, whereas a conventional projectile is ignited through a gunpowder charge in the cartridge?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. We have the gunpowder charge which is either in the cartridge or is freely filled. There are two types of charge and the way the projectiles are filled with the charge. Some do have cartridges, others do not; they have free gunpowder charges. So in a conventional projectile the fuel, if you like to call it, is in the form of gunpowder charge, which is either in a cartridge or is placed -- several of these charges are placed in the gunpowder chamber. If you're dealing with a rocket projectile of the Orkan type, then this projectile has an energy motor and gives it an initial velocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the type of charge, am I correct in saying, when I quote from your report, when you say that the principle of the trajectory flight is the same regardless of what set it off, whether it was set off by a rocket motor or a gunpowder charge. The trajectory is always the same, just like a conventional projectile, and it cannot be influenced once it discharged. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When you fire a projectile or launch a projectile, whichever word you like to use, you can have no more influence during the flight, the trajectory and flight. That is true of Orkan as well. The only difference is that Orkan has the rocket motor which sets it into motion. And this rocket motor launches the projectile, giving it its initial velocity, which is 4.3 seconds of burning. After the 4.3 seconds, the projectile gains its own initial velocity and follows its flight and trajectory just like any other conventional projectile would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When we say that the projectile flies in the same way as a conventional projectile, and you say that you cannot influence its flight, does that mean that you cannot correct, make any corrections of the trajectory in flight or guide the rocket in any other way towards the target. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the rocket is launched, you can have no more influence on the trajectory in flight. All that can affect it are the meteorological conditions which occur along the trajectory when the trajectory is in flight, but the crew, Orkan's crew, for example, or some other artillery system crew can have no further influence on the flight or the trajectory of the projectile that has been launched towards a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the explanation you've just gave what is interesting to note is this: You say that with the Orkan rocket system there is a camera which films the active portion of the rocket's flight and automatically corrects elements for the next projectile, for the next rocket. Now, a -- conventional artillery projectiles don't have that type of camera, do they?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Orkan was the only system to have this camera, which in fact filmed the projectile's flight, filmed from the launcher and from the neighboring launcher. You can film the active portion of the projectile's flight from the moment it is launched out of a barrel for the 4.3 seconds that the rocket motor is in operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in respect of this answer you go on to say -- what you've just said, actually, that with the conventional type of artillery as well as with the other two multiple-barrelled rocket launchers which were part of the weapons of the Serb army in Krajina, the M-63 Plamen system and the Oganj system, the correction was done by guidance, reconnaissance and guidance, whereas Orkan has this camera. So it's only Orkan that has the camera. Is that right? Is that indisputable, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That will be -- that will suffice, thank you, your answer yes. Now, the existence of the camera recording the active section of the flight has as its task to automatically correct the data for the next rocket. Does that, in fact, mean that this was a modern solution to the rocket which enables very precise artillery firing, as precise as possible?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system for calculating the trajectory, theoretical trajectory calculations on the basis of data coming in, ballistical data, meteorological conditions, all this incorporated, as such it has memory and memorises the trajectory in that way. When a rocket is launched, that rocket, its active -- the active section of the flight is recorded by the camera while the rocket motor is functioning. The system compares the theoretical trajectory with the actual trajectory, the trajectory in flight. And it is able automatically to correct even before the next rocket is launched, to correct and adjust the calculations so that the trajectory of the rocket is improved. And we must also bear in mind that regardless of the exactitude of the firing elements, even if you determine them very precisely, all the elements of firing, does not guarantee that this calculated theoretical trajectory will correspond to the actual trajectory because errors -- there will be errors in the theoretical calculations of probability, just as you have dispersion, and there are errors that are made in preparing the initial elements so that we cannot say that we have calculated the trajectory which would be 100 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje. That was a very detailed answer, but the sense of my question was this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before you go on, Mr. Milovancevic, and this had occurred to me before. Based on what you have said, Mr. Poje, what is the margin of error? Can you say here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this, Your Honour. To prepare the initial elements you would have to gather data and information for firing, the processing of that data and information as well, and then to adjust this on the launcher, incorporate this information on the launcher itself. When you're doing all these three things there are errors, and these errors will depend on a number of elements. The construction, the design itself, the tolerance when the system is designed, the way in which the measurements are taken, the instruments that you're using to make these measurements. All these have margins of errors. When you have a lot of these errors, you come to what we call a summary error, which is in the initial errors. There are some errors that we cannot influence that are relatively small. We don't know the direction or the size exactly because it is the theory of probability that deals with elements of that nature. The theory of firing, according to Zivanov, speaks about these errors in the preparation of these input elements. The most exact way of preparing your input is by conducting full and complete preparation, and a better way is to correct your elements, correcting the elements, making corrections with your input elements. So we come back to the preparation stage. Complete and full preparation is the best way of determining the initial elements for firing, which incorporate exact coordinates, exact ballistic information, and exact meteorological information. And regardless of all this, even if you have all these very exact data, a summary element in the preparation is from .08 to 1.2 per cent of the distance or range of firing. So that's the margin of error. And we have turned that into Vd values, and I'm talking about dispersion in line, which is equal to 2 Vd, dispersion in range --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So even if you have the most exact way of preparation, the margin or error is 2 Vd. The overall image of error or error chart is plus/minus 4 mean errors, or average errors, which means that errors in the initial elements is relatively large, there's a relatively large margin of error, and that means at long distances, long ranges, you have to undertake a correction in firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the correction and the camera that we mentioned and the question that the Judge asked you, we're talking about one basic topic. The basic condition in artillery firing is to hit the target with a projectile. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, to hit the target successfully you say we need to have full and complete preparation, and you also said that for that precision the correction of firing is very important. Now, with the Orkan system, this is done automatically by using a camera. A camera records the active section of the flight and automatically corrects the data of the next rocket. Now, my next question is that the most up-to-date modern solution that you found?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can have classical correction with the Orkan as well, conventional correction. All you have to do is to see how you have fired and whether you have hit the target. So, as we say, we can use a camera. That's the difference. You can use a camera to record the trajectory and then make automatic corrections, on the assumption that you have calculated the correct trajectory because if the -- if we have not taken into account all the parameters, all the initial firing data, the topographical data, the meteorological data, and if you have calculated your trajectory wrongly, then when the camera is used the actual trajectory will give you a false record, a false trajectory, if I can put it that way, call it a false one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje. You've explained that to us in great detail, and my question boils down to this: This is automatic correction during flight and that that is made possible by electronics, the camera, the recording camera, with the sole aim of ensuring as precise targeting and firing as possible. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But may I just add this with your permission, that regardless with the correction, automatic correction, there is still corrections that are made but they are 50 per cent less than the errors you would be making in the initial firing data, .08 to 1.1 Vd or dispersion in range.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje. Now, on page 23 of the B/C/S, or 19 in the English, you talk about a rocket projectile and state that it impacts on the target with a warhead and the principle is not -- no different from a classical projectile because just like a conventional projectile the rocket projectile as well contains a warhead which has its fuse, explosive charge, and all the rest of the elements. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And if you look at the bottom it says: Modern projectiles have cluster warheads with cumulative bomblets and the other fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje, that deals with my next question. But in relation to that answer of yours, we come back to a question we raised yesterday, and this is this: Orkan as a multiple-barrelled rocket launcher has two types of rockets when we look at the warhead and both rockets have cluster charges. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know and on the basis of the literature I've studied, Orkan does, indeed, have two types of warheads, one rocket with two types of warhead, the cluster warhead with the bomblets, and the cluster warhead with armoured shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just repeat. The warhead that was used in the targets in Zagreb was the cluster warhead with cumulative cluster fragments, whereas the other has anti-armoured mines which weren't used, nor would there have been any sense in using this in targeting certain features in Zagreb. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because the cluster warhead was used -- it affected live force, whereas the cluster warheads are used to lay minefields at a distance. And they were mostly used to prevent armoured vehicles and units with armoured vehicles breaking through along certain axes precipitously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to that answer of yours, am I right in saying that the only rocket which you could use for targets in Zagreb was precisely the type that was used, with this kind of warhead?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the data that I had at my disposal, what was launched on Zagreb were cluster warheads, rockets with cluster warheads containing the bomblets. No other type of rocket was launched. That was the only type of rocket launched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What were the targets in Zagreb? The question is put to you, Mr. Milovancevic, because I don't think the witness knows what the intended targets were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can answer this in two ways. I can give you a direct answer, but I think that will influence the course of my cross-examination of this witness. But I will be asking very specific questions to the witness about that which will give you an answer. If you're not satisfied with my questions and the witness's answer, I will give you a direct answer, but that's the only reason I'm a bit reticent in jumping the gun and talking about that now. It would have a material influence on the contents of the witness's further testimony during the cross-examination and my questions that are to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, let's find out. Now, your question was: In relation to that answer of yours, am I right in saying that the only rocket which you could use for targeting Zagreb was precisely the type that was used with this kind of warhead? Now, before this witness can answer, I would like to be satisfied that he knows what the target is because otherwise how does he answer this kind of question? Mr. Poje, do you know what the targets were in Zagreb? Just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't really know which the specific targets were. On the basis of the information I was given and I had at my disposal, I just dealt with the location these projectiles were activated and the areas where these bomblets from the cluster warheads from the rocket fell on Zagreb. Now, what the actual target or targets were when Zagreb was targeted, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see the problem? This witness can't answer that question unless he knows the intended target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think there's any problem, actually, because the witness in his expert report said that a possible target was the civilian population, for instance, according to the police reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if he has said that, my question to him would be linked to that statement of his, so that is why I said a moment ago that I would like to leave these questions to a later stage of the cross-examination, not to avoid having him answer your question. And with your permission might I be allowed to continue my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not allowed just yet. He tells us "possible targets." Now, possible -- he's obviously guessing based on the type of rocket that was used. You are telling him that the targets that were intended to be hit could only be hit if you used this type of rocket. Now, you've got to tell him what were the intended targets. He's telling us what the possible targets were. Therefore, until and unless he knows what the intended target is, there is no way he can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm starting out from the allegations made in the indictment, according to which the expert's statements are taken into account where he says that in his opinion the targets were the civilian population. Now, if that answer of his is something that is contained in his expert report, my question to him was: Can you attack a civilian population with anti-tank shells or some other type of projectile?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The target you're talking about is the target he is talking about in his report, that -- namely, the civilian populations. Say that to him. Then he will be able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not what I am saying, Your Honour. I am claiming that that is not so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then what are you saying? You're saying he is postulating a possible target in his report and that is -- because he is postulating that that is what you are asking him about. Now tell him: That in your report you are postulating this kind of a -- this kind of target and could that target be struck only by the use of this kind of rocket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Also your question before, in transcript 15, line 6, you asked if this wouldn't be the only instrument to make any sense in using this in targeting certain features in Zagreb, and this was also a little unclear; therefore, the question: Is this right, was to me also disturbing. And the answer: Yes, didn't say very much. This is the same line of problem I would see there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think there's a problem in the transcript. I'm going to withdraw my previous question for us to be able to deal with the normal cross-examination of this witness according to the order that he follows in his expert report. And then I'll ask the other question later on with your permission and indulgence so that we don't come into a situation where I can, by my answer, pre-empt -- by my question can pre-empt an answer. So with your permission, may I continue along the lines my cross-examination was following which was following the order set out in the witness report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means for as long as you are not going to ask the witness to answer questions which -- about which he needs to have data first before he can answer. And you're asking the question without supplying him with the data, okay, and the data being the target here. You may proceed. So that question is disallowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I withdrew the question and I do accept your ruling. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 24 of the B/C/S of your report, or page 20 in English, in footnote 6 you talk about the fragmentation effect of the projectile and that you say that this is the effect which is gained by the lethal fragments of the shell or projectile.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we have a reference, please, for footnote 6, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every projectile, anti-tank shells, do have the fragmentation effect, the only difference being that this fragmentation effect is achieved with the casing of the projectile itself or part of the casing in conventional weapons or with the balls or pellets from the bomblet in the Orkan example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph underneath this you talk about the fragmentation effect upon delayed fire. You mentioned delayed fire yesterday and you explained that with -- in order to achieve fragmentation effect at impact, the fuse is adjusted to this effect -- slowing down effect --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please give the interpreters a reference because we don't seem to find it on the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the witnesses are asking for assistance from you -- I beg your pardon, the interpreters are asking that you give them a reference, please. They are not able to follow what you are doing -- what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the beginning of my question, and I apologise if I wasn't precise enough, I said it was page 24 in the B/C/S or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or page 20 in the English, but page 20 -- and at page 20, we don't see any footnote 6 and that is why the interpreters are having difficulties.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You could say in which chapter we are, the chapter number --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, just looking between the two versions, the original and the translation, it looks like the English version footnote 7 should be footnote 6, so that may be an error in the translation. In any effect, I believe what counsel is referring to is the bottom of page 19 in the English and moving to the top of page 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That may very well be so because footnote 6 is at page 13, very far from where you are in the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think that's an error in the translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And this footnote in fact corresponds with footnote 6 in the B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I hope the interpreters are now in line with you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As I was saying we were dealing with chapter 3.6 entitled "fragmentation effect of a projectile." And we're dealing with paragraph 7 of that chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd like to ask the Court to bear in mind that there really does seem to be a difference in the footnotes, the numbers in the B/C/S and the English, and that is unfortunate, which is the reason for the misunderstanding. So it wasn't an intentional thing on my part, or mistake on my part, just to understand the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Nothing of the sort is suggested, Mr. Milovancevic. You -- it is understood it was not your fault. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's not what I meant. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in that chapter you're talking about the fragmentation effect of a projectile, let me repeat the question because there's been quite a lot of time gone by, that that can be with -- fuses set instantaneous action or delayed action and the fuse is adjusted accordingly. The fuse is set for instantaneous action or delayed action, is that right, for impact and time fire?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May we look at page 28 now in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That should be in English page 23, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On this page in the B/C/S we have a paragraph beginning "time fire." And above that paragraph about time fire, there's a sentence that I'm interested in. You say that: "In order to increase the effect in addition -- or rather, time fire can be used to increase the fragmentation effect of a projectile." And you go on to explain that that time fire is delivered with a delayed-action projectile which enables projectile bursts on the trajectory at a certain height above the target. So is that the essence of this time fire in artillery firing?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a conventional projectile time fire is delivered with a fuge projectile and a fuse, a time-fuse, in such a way that the explosion occurs at a certain height above the target. That is what we mean when we're talking about conventional artillery time fire. If we look at the Orkan system, on the other hand, we have to differentiate between two types of fuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Mr. Poje --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you -- may I interrupt you, Mr. Milovancevic. You've quoted something to the witness and you said what you are quoting is above the paragraph starting with "time fire." And I am desperately trying to find what it is you are trying to quoting. The quotation reads: "In order to increase the effect in addition -- or rather, time fire can be used to increase the fragmentation effect of a projectile." Now I'm trying to find that. "In addition to ricochet fire and unconcealed personnel, it is also possible to use time fire to increase the fragmentation effect." That's what I see on the sentence above "time fire," which is not what you said to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, the -- I would like to be with you. I would like to know what it is you are quoting to the witness so that I follow your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand your dilemma, Your Honour. May I explain this through questions to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, just refer -- no, no, just refer me on the page to what it is you were quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sentence you just read out, Your Honour. "In addition to ricochet fire at unconcealed personnel, it is also possible to use time fire to increase the fragmentation effect." That is the sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, that's not what is quoted here on the transcript, Mr. Milovancevic. What is quoted on the transcript says: "In order to increase the effect in addition -- or rather, time fire can be used to increase the fragmentation effect of a projectile." There's no mention of ricochet or personnel or unconcealed thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, and that need not be mentioned because the sense of my question was along those lines, and I was referring to the topic of time fire. So I just referred to that portion of his text which was in -- we were interested in. So I wasn't referring to ricochet fire but time fire. Ricochet fire wasn't the point I was interested in. The material sense of time fire, why it is used. That's what I wanted to ask the witness, and that is why I just read out a part of the sentence, the part of the sentence that I wanted to focus on, not the first part with ricochet fire. But I can reformulate the question to make the transcript clearer, so there's no misunderstanding with respect to the actual text in the expert report and the other words used in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The only problem is when you do quote, quote correctly, then we know where you are and what you're saying. Don't paraphrase and then put quotation marks because there are quotation marks in here. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, I apologise for this break. I partly paraphrased and partly quoted, in the belief that I was not actually misinterpreting the text before we; however, I will be more precise following His Honour's instructions. Let me repeat my question. Can one say that it's also possible to use time fire in order to increase the fragmentation effect?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Time fire is used to neutralise personnel out in the open, and it's more effective than impact firing. A combination of impact and time fire is often used to neutralise unconcealed personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When speaking about time fire used to increase the fragmentation effect, you say in your text that it is delivered with a delayed-action projectile with a time or proximity fuse, so that the projectile bursts on the trajectory at a certain height above the target. Is that what time fire is used for?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Using a fuge warhead and a time-fuse, this is used with the aim of having an explosion, a burst, at a certain height above the target which causes fragments to fall on the personnel on the ground or the live force on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is precisely why I asked this question. This automatically leads us to figure 11, portraying time fire, and it's on page 23 of the text in English and on page 28 of the text in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have this photograph before you with the title "time fire"? The slanting line with a little cloud at the end of it is supposed to represent a trajectory of projectile adjusted for time fire. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the trajectory, and at the end of it above the target you see the explosion of the time projectile which takes place because of a certain adjustment of the delayed-action fuse or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that time fire is done in such a way that the explosion is at the most favourable possible height above the target and that this produces an effect which is three times stronger. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. When using conventional artillery ammunition in time fire, using delayed-action fuses and proximity fuses, the dispersion at a height is very small, both theoretically and in practice. And this increases the efficacy two or three times against personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As the very purpose of this kind of firing is to have an explosion at a certain height above the target, and we can see this in figure 11, let me remind you of Exhibit 771, showing a similar trajectory of an Orkan projectile opening at the certain height above the target, 800 to 1000 metres higher. These are two completely different things, are they not?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Speaking about time fire here, we are talking about the conventional type of time fire. In the Orkan system we have two kinds of fuses. In the rocket itself, there is a time-fuse which makes it possible for the warhead to open at a certain height, 800 to 1.000 metres. That's one kind of fuse. The other kind of -- the first kind is in the warhead itself. And the second kind of fuse is found in every bomblet. It makes it possible for every bomblet to be set off on impact. So those are impact fuses. There is -- in the cluster warhead itself is one fuse, and there are impact fuses in each bomblet in addition, which set the bomblet off on impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show Exhibit 771, please, on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So what we see before us on the monitor is a situation when the casing of the rocket opens up and bomblets fall out. But this is not the explosion we see in figure 11, in the case of time fire. Is this beyond dispute, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. These two diagrams, figure 11 in the report and figure now on the monitor, are different. What we see on the monitor is a fuse, the task of which is to open the cluster warhead, to open it up, and release, so to say, 288 bomblets, which are supplied with impact fuses. These bomblets are activated by these impact fuses. They explode on impact with an obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To round off this topic, which I think is very important, does this answer mean that what we have in Exhibit 771 on the monitor shows the dispersion of the bomblets which takes place at a height of 800 to 1.000 metres, and this is not the explosion of the bomblets in the Orkan. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we have to understand is that the explosive charge which is activated in the cluster warhead is such that it only opens the warhead and releases the bomblets. This is not the conventional fuge charge because the warhead is filled with bomblets, that's a cluster warhead. So the explosion is only sufficient to open up the warhead and release the 288 bomblets which fall towards the target.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel not overlap with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the bomblets fall on any kind of obstacle, the impact fuse is activated, it causes the explosion of the bomblet. And then the double effect is achieved. The action of the balls and the action of the cumulative blast piercing the obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's move on to the next topic. The next chapter deals with the Orkan system, and we've already said that it has two kinds of cluster warheads. You explained the number of cumulative fragmentation bomblets in the cluster warhead equipped with bomblets. And you also said that the calibre of a bomblet is 40 millimetres and that it pierces armoured steel, which is 60 millimetres thick. That is very high piercing power.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cumulative blast pierces the armour of every modern tank from above -- from on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can such bomblets with their impact blast and destructive action also destroy buildings?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, it's possible. Although they are primarily intended to pierce tanks, armoured personnel carriers, armoured vehicles, other projectiles are used to hit bunkers, dug-outs, fortified buildings, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are all these goals against which the Orkan rocket can be used?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, these are all the targets that are targeted by such weapons, armoured vehicles and other targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In chapter 3.7, which deals with accuracy of artillery fire, it's page 30 in B/C/S, you say when dealing with the concept of artillery fire that it: "Is the action of artillery projectiles on the target for the purpose of producing desired material and moral effects." When you define artillery fire in this manner, does this definition also apply to the Orkan rocket system?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Any projectile action is aimed at producing desired material and also moral effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you speak about the moral effects or the psychological effects, is it demoralising for the opposite side because of the forceful sudden precise artillery action, in this case of the Orkan rocket?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to say that in the case of artillery fire, including Orkan, there are material effects, but we know that not every projectile hits its target. However, a vast number of explosions is produced, a lot of smoke. And in any case this is demoralising for the people in the area targeted. For example, on the Slunj training field we fired on the resistance point of a platoon which was defending the area, and we established that there were relatively few direct hits, but when we looked at the effect of this fire, everything was shaking, everything was smoking, burning, and this had to have a huge demoralising effect for the people. Of course there were dummies there, not real people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this might be a convenient moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is a convenient moment for a break. Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We'll break until quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We left off at chapter 3.7 entitled "accuracy of artillery fire," and we spoke about the action of artillery projectiles to produce desired material and moral effects. You go on to say that the purpose of an artillery firing is to carry out the following combat tasks: Neutralisation, destruction, demolition, interdiction, and harassment. And you go on to say that artillery fire must be sudden, accurate, powerful, and brief. Are these the general rules of artillery fire which also applied to the Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they applied to all artillery and therefore they applied to the Orkan as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: A few pages before that on page 34 in B/C/S and -- you say -- you speak about artillery fire. You say that artillery fire has three stages, the preparation of initial firing data, correction, and group firing. The preparation of the initial firing data makes it possible to have elements as precise as possible to begin correction and to begin group firing. Does this also refer to the Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is both for -- this also applies to the Orkan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a precise reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You then go on to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you referred the witness to page 34 I think of the B/C/S, and the interpreters want to know a correct reference I suppose in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is the text above 3.7.2, and the title is "accuracy of artillery fire." I will check the page number in English. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's the bottom of page 27 in the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm grateful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 27, when you speak about adjustment, you say that a fire adjustment eliminates errors in preparing initial data and provides the most accurate possible data for a group firing. I will remind you of one of my previous questions. I wish to know whether the adjustment in the case of the Orkan system is carried out by means of the camera which is in the rocket and which sends back data for the automatic adjustment of the following projectiles. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, compared to other conventional artillery weapons in which adjustment is carried out from observation posts, the Orkan, with its system, makes it possible to carry out adjustment without carrying out observation, from an observation post. A camera is used which films the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for interrupting you, but this is repetitious now. Thank you. In chapter 3.7.2 entitled "accuracy of artillery fire," you deal with the precision of artillery fire and you speak about accidental or inevitable errors which have multiple causes, and it is not possible to observe and analyse them fully. My question is: Is this a characteristic of all artillery fire, including Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a characteristic of every fire because there are very many accidental errors on which we can have no influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with these errors, Mr. Poje, on page 36 of the B/C/S, which is page 29 of the English text, you give a table showing the errors in preparing data for a group firing. On the left-hand side of the table, the heading is "method for determining data," and on the right-hand side the title is "mean error," or the heading. And you link these two elements. Do you see the table before you?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the method for determining data, the three last columns or rows are full preparation, shortened preparation, and simple preparation. When you compare these with the figures in the right-hand column, is it clear from this table that the fuller the preparation the more precise the fire, or vice versa? The simpler the preparation, the less precise the fire. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correctness of the elements for fire depend on the data. The fuller the preparation, the smaller the mean error, and out of the three methods that can be used in firing, the most precise is in the case of full preparation and the least precise is in the case of simple preparation. The mean error is the smallest with full preparation and the highest with simple preparation of initial firing data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The general rules for the use of artillery, do they provide that full preparation of initial firing data is always required at distances longer than 20 kilometres? I think you wrote something about this in your wrote.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At distances up to six kilometres one can use simple preparation. At distances of up to 20 kilometres, full preparation is required but shortened preparation is also possible. Over 20 kilometres, full preparation of initial firing data is mandatory. When firing at distances of over 20 kilometres, the initial firing data must be done so that there is full preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 29 there is another diagram showing the probability that the mean error in preparation and so on, and underneath is a text which says that the: "Artillery rules of preparation say that full preparation is mandatory at distances over 20 kilometres" and that this also applies to the Orkan.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It applies to all artillery system. If the firing distance is over 20 kilometres, the full preparation of initial firing data is mandatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next chapter you speak about - and that's 3.7.3 - you speak about the influence of various factors on the effectiveness of a firing. And the chapter that follows this is entitled -- well, it's 3.7.5, and the title is "effectiveness of a firing." That's page 41 in the B/C/S. I'll try to find the page reference in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's page 33, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When discussing the effectiveness of the firing, you say that it depends on a large number of factors, the most important of which are, and I will point to some things, the dimensions, shape, and nature of the target. And then in one of these bullet points you say that the effectiveness of the firing also depends on the appropriate selection of the type of projectile, fuse, charge, trajectory, shape, and the type of firing. Do these general provisions also apply to the Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effectiveness of firing, these apply to artillery in general, not a particular artillery piece. The effectiveness of firing depends on all the factors listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your expert report in chapter 3.7.5, discussing the effectiveness of firing, and when we come to the end of this chapter, at the very end of this chapter, which is page 44 of the English text, before you go on to 3.8, "purpose and main characteristics of the Orkan," you discuss an example of firing from an Orkan. Do you see the page where it says: Example 2, the firing conditions are as in Example 1. Example 1 discusses battery firing. And you say that the target is partially concealed. And then you go on to say, I quote: "In view of the type of ammunition" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I regret having to interrupt but I'm not there with you. I'm -- I'd like to know what page it is in the English version, because at 3.8, the heading is "purpose and main characteristics of a VBR," and there is a 3.8.1 which doesn't have the caption that you have referred to. Could you help me, please, to get to the point where you are with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I regret having caused this confusion. We are on page 36 of the text in English, and this is just before the text dealing with the Orkan. So this is page 36 of the text in English. On this page, 36 of the English text, there is discussion of Example 2, and the two last paragraphs referring to Example 2 are the topic we are dealing with now, Your Honour. I believe that we have now oriented ourselves. I omitted to mark every B/C/S page with the equivalent English page, and that's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- when dealing with example 2 you say: "The same type of ammunition may be used," you're referring to the Orkan rocket system, "for both personnel and weapons under cover," and you say -- or "unconcealed." And you say: "Unnatural, artificial, including armoured personnel carriers, armoured and other vehicles, buildings, et cetera." Does this mean that this warhead, cluster warhead, containing 288 bomblets is effective both against personnel and against armoured vehicles as well as against buildings and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next page refers to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please switch on his microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- the Orkan system. Excuse me. The next page refers to the characteristics of the Orkan. And you say that this was a system developed by the end of 1985 by Yugoslav and Iraqi experts. Where did you get this information about the Iraqi experts?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Orkan was tested in Iraq. A large number of projectiles were fired there, and I have mentioned the source of my information here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is this source the Pentagon?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the fact that a system was tested in Iraq need not automatically mean that it was developed in collaboration with Iraq. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree in part, but if a country participated in the testing of a system then most likely its experts were working on this system as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any sense in which the participation of Iraqi experts influences the technical and tactical characteristics of this system in a negative way?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because regardless of which experts worked on it, the Orkan was developed on the territory of the former Yugoslavia and the leaders of this development were Yugoslav experts. As the Orkan was tested in Iraq, most likely Iraqi experts also participated in developing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say on the first page where you deal with the Orkan that the prototypes were tested by the end of 1985 and two years later the Orkan was introduced into operational use in the JNA. This period of development and testing from 1980 to 1987 was a period when the democratic west supported Iraqi armed operations against Iran, and that France, Great Britain, and the USA were on the Iraqi side in that conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in one stage western Europe and Yugoslavia as well supported Iraq in its fight against Iran, and it was probably at that time that the Iraqi army was supplied with western arms systems. As far as I know and in my conversations with the experts dealing with the Orkan, Orkan was supplied to the armed forces of Iraq.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now move on to talk about the technical characteristics of the Orkan. And you say on the next page: "The M87 Orkan self-propelled long-range multiple rocket launching system has the function of providing fire support to corps-sized and army-sized units." In view of the fact that this is a long-range system, does it also act against shorter ranges, 1 to 50, 50 to 200, and 200 and above?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said that the Orkan is in between medium-range and long-range weapons. It's at the end of the medium-range scale and at the end of the long-range scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you speak about its range, you say that it can effectively neutralise all kinds of targets and provide anti-armoured barrage fire, firing rockets with a cluster warhead containing anti- armour mines. This is a general characteristic of the Orkan. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we discussed the Orkan as a system, in view of the fact that it has two kinds of warheads, one kind with bomblets intended to neutralise and destroy personnel and equipment, and another kind which contains anti-tank mines and it can be used to combat tanks and other armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you go on to say that bearing in mind the relatively large dispersion pattern of the Orkan, it is not a particularly suitable weapon for use against populated areas. When you say it is not a particularly suitable weapon, does this mean that its use against an inhabited area is excluded or is it possible?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact of the large dispersion pattern, the selection of targets in an inhabited area has to be very thorough. This does not exclude the possibility of using the Orkan against military targets in an inhabited area. Military targets also have to be carefully selected, and firing on such targets must be such that there are no hits outside those targets. The selection of the target is crucial in the case of firing an Orkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in continuation of that text under the heading of "Orkan multiple rocket launcher," you talk about its tactical and technical features and so on and a system for leveling, assuming positions, for setting into motion launchers, and you say that everything is linked with digital commands and that all these systems can be handled by the crew in the launcher. Now, do these characteristics speak of its computerisation and maximum effectiveness in the sense of technical solutions, the ones set out here?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orkan, but we're just talking about a launcher here, which is a modern weapon, which include -- which means that you can take up your firing positions quickly and that you have all the possibilities of effecting proper firing from the cabin itself. The crew does not have to leave its cabin and prepare the weapon to go into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you spoke about the technical characteristics you said that there was a command vehicle or the fact that each vehicle can -- could be used as a commander and computer centre, and that is the characteristic of Orkan, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every Orkan unit has a vehicle which houses the computer or computer system by means of which it is possible on the basis of initial data that I've already mentioned to calculate the -- on the basis of algorithms, initial elements and so on, they are conveyed to the launcher itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in continuation of the text we have figure 14 on page 49 of the B/C/S text, and figure 49 [as interpreted] is the trajectory passage of adjustment rocket launched through a reference plain in space. And in continuation of the text, about Orkan can you say that a television adjustor, which consists of a television camera, which functions in the visible and closed infra-red range and has a monitor and a computer enables automatic adjustment. That is the automatic adjustment that we spoke about earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We talked about the camera, that it records the active phase of the flight of the rocket and trajectory, and by comparing both trajectories is able to correct the trajectory for the following rocket, next rocket, to be launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje. Now, in continuation of that text you look at the rocket for the rocket system of Orkan. You look at the rocket itself. Now, since we dealt with that topic, I don't want to waste time. I think we've seen to that. Then you talk about the system -- the direction of fire, and you show us the component parts of the individual units of the system. We have the picture of a truck that looks like a very ordinary truck; it is page 54 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we have an English reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So that with respect to these tactical and technical characteristics of Orkan, I'm not going to ask you any more questions about that. Now, after the Orkan, and it is 3.8.3, the next chapter, 3.8.3, you deal with the 128-millimetre M-63 Plamen multiple rocket launcher. I'm not going to follow the text in detail there; I'm just going to ask you one question. It is a multiple rocket launcher, which is one of the weapons that the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina had, and the rocket range is about eight kilometres. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: 8.600 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Right, 8.600 metres. Thank you. Now, in addition to that Plamen multiple rocket launcher, which is on wheels and has 32 rockets, you also dealt with the Oganj weapon, which is also 120 millimetres but with a longer range. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And that Oganj has a 120-kilometre range. That is also one of the weapons that the Republic of Srpska Krajina had. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention for a few moments on chapter 3.9, Mr. Poje, entitled "artillery groups, command and control." Page 63 of the B/C/S and it says "artillery groups" and "control and command" -- "command and control."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is page 53 of the English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We're not going to go through all the individual sections of that chapter. I'm just interested in the beginning of the following -- or rather, I'm interested in point 3.9.2, "command and control," and it comes underneath a table. So it is 3.9.2, "command and control," page 64 of the B/C/S. In that chapter, 3.9.2, you explain who it is who is in command of the artillery fire, and you say that commanding the artillery is the task of the commanders and commands of joint tactical and operational units and the commands of artillery units. Is that so? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in continuation of that same chapter, 3.9.2, paragraph 2, you emphasise that the artillery is commanded by the commander of a joint tactical and operational unit directly or through his chief of artillery. So that's a general provision about the functioning of the artillery, and does it correspond -- does it apply to Orkan, too?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a branch of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in connection with that answer of yours my next question is this: Can we therefore say that the artillery never acts alone? It functions within the framework of a set composition, and it is commanded by the commander of a joint tactical or operational group directly or through the chief of artillery to which orders are issued?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to explain? According to the rules of artillery, there are rules governing the command and control of firing, and that is a component part of command and control which relates to firing itself. That is in the briefest possible terms. Now, what happens to the management, or how firing is determined, you determine fire assignments and tasks and their effects on individual units and artillery units to be deployed. Artillery units, infantry units, armoured vehicle units. Now, who is in charge of fire? It is the commanders of the support units who are in charge of the fire. Now, handling fire means the firing itself. In simple terms, it is the execution of the firing itself. So the commander of the support unit issues assignments. If I am the commander of an artillery unit, I am duty-bound, on the basis of my professional capabilities and the equipment I have, to effect firing. Now, who handles the firing itself? It is the commanders of the artillery units and leaders of the artillery units and observers, reconnaissance men, who are trained to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now following on from your answer there you go on to quote provisions on the use of the VSK 1995 and orders by the Main Staff of the Serb Army of Krajina about raising combat-readiness. Now, from those two documents you draw the conclusion and say that: "We can see that the Orkan department received assignments from the command of the Main Staff of the R -- SVK, or rather, Colonel Djilas." In the form of Colonel Djilas. So my question is: Could Orkan have gone into operation only pursuant to the command of the Main Staff or Colonel Djilas?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the documents that I had at my disposal, they are three documents, you mentioned two of those documents, the directive and raising combat -- increasing combat-readiness, and moving the Orkan to a new location was the third document. In all these three documents it says that the assignments to Orkan are issued by the Main Staff commander, the commander of the Serb Army of Krajina, and I think in two documents it says "or Colonel Djilas." So the Main Staff SVK commander or Colonel Djilas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 68 of your report, or 58 of the English version, we come to chapter 4, and the title of that chapter is "doctrine of using fire support." And then within the frameworks of chapter 4 you address planning artillery firings. And you say that: "The planning of artillery firings includes a number of activities performed by artillery commands and other commands to ensure the most successful action of their units." And further on under point 4.2 you say that: "The commanders of joint tactical and operational units have the sole right to use artillery in combat," and that applies to Orkan, too. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said, the deployment of the artillery and artillery assignments as well as other support units, orders come from the commander of the support unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that was chapter 4.2. Then one page later we come to chapter 4.3, "target selection." And you say that: "Target selection includes determining the purpose of using artillery," and you explain that by saying further down in the text that: "Inflicting the greatest possible losses on the enemy, especially losses in personnel, must be the main measure for selecting the target." Does that apply to all artillery, including Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true for all artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And finally for the purpose of using the artillery, in the last sentence it says: "A good selection of artillery targets should inflict direct and gradually possible losses on the enemy thereby breaking its combat capability and defeating it and destroying it completely." So that includes all the combat activity, including artilleries?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the actions of the units to inflict as many losses on the enemy as possible with respect to breaking his combat capability and make it impossible for the enemy to act in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now the next chapter, chapter 5, "use of artillery support in populated areas." Under 5.1, on page 70 of the B/C/S, you refer to the provisions of the combat rules of the artillery of the former JNA, of which you were a member of, were you not, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In continuation of the text you explain that: "The action of artillery during an attack on a populated locality is affected by a number of factors." And then in the following paragraph you say: "The action is mainly delivered through direct fire in a populated locality." And you go on to explain that to neutralise and to destroy a large number of targets it is necessary to cause partial damage to buildings and other structures. That then is the characteristic of direct fire for all artillery systems. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you use direct fire on a populated area, you have to know that most often the targets are -- or rather, that the personnel and the vehicles or -- are usually obstructed by buildings. So the features and buildings are destroyed in the process, and the rules speak about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And below that we see that: "Indirect fire in populated areas is limited by difficulties in organising observation activities, monitoring combat development, and maintaining communications." And that is the characteristic of every artillery indirect fire. Right, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you are attacking a populated area, then those are the problems the artillery encounters when it opens fire on a populated area of that type.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, four paragraphs below that you state, and that is page 71 of the B/C/S, that: "The units of the Army of Srpska Krajina did not conduct an attack on the city of Zagreb.
