This means that the Orkan had no need to conduct direct support operations but was conducting general support operations." And when you say that, you mean the effects of the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995. Is that what it's about?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said yesterday that there were two types of support, direct support and general support. And direct support is support which directly affects the operations of a unit on a battle-field; a brigade attacking, for example. All the firing conducted for the needs of that brigade to carry out its assignment successfully. That is direct fire. Then we have the other type of general artillery support, which is resorted to against targets which are not demonstrating -- or rather, are not firing at the units on the front but could at some other point in time, a day or two later, or later on, can attack or fire at the unit in question, which means that on that 2nd and 3rd of May we could say that it was general support that was being given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In continuation of that paragraph where you speak about general support of Orkan against targets in Zagreb, you say: "Most probably that was used to instill fear in the population, its property, and the infrastructure." When you say most probably that was so, does that mean that you didn't have a document on the basis of which you were able to establish what the real object of the operation was?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we discussed that already today. Realistically speaking, I did not have any information or data as to what those military targets were and what targets were targeted in Zagreb. All the information I had told me where the projectiles were located or, rather, where parts of the rocket projectiles were located and where the bomblets fell. Now, what the actual target was, in my final conclusion I state that I don't know what the military target was in fact, but I claim something else, and that is that even if military targets were aimed at, were targeted, that it was risky to target them because the dispersion pattern is very large and that in examples of this kind it was to be expected that the targeting would have its effect on the civilian population as well as buildings, vehicles, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What -- can I just ask. What kind of artillery could have been used to avoid that wide dispersion result?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very hard to say. It's very hard to say what could have been used and what the Serb Army of the Krajina had at its disposal at the time. To attack military targets in a populated area, the best weapon to use would be only guided missiles, because their dispersion pattern is very narrow and they hit either the very centre or very close to the centre of the target point. Any other kind of artillery used at long range has a very wide dispersion pattern, and this applies especially to multiple-barrelled rocket launchers, which by their nature have a very wide dispersion pattern. So let me repeat: In order to aim at targets in a populated area, only guided projectiles or self-guided projectiles should be used. Those are the best kind of projectiles to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Any of the projectiles you have discussed in this report could be used, apart from the multi-barrelled one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the range, which is 40, 45, to 50 kilometres, the Orkan was an artillery piece that can be used at such a large distance. As for other artillery pieces, I don't know whether they had them or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the question. The question is: What could have been appropriately used. Whether or not they had them is -- we don't know. You also don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to point out once again that in such a case the most effective and best projectiles to use are self-guided or guided projectiles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the Orkan, although it could be used, it would have the effect of a very wide dispersion area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we've already said, the dispersion pattern of the Orkan is very great. This means that when firing at a military target in a densely populated area, such as Zagreb for example, it was to be expected that some of the projectiles would fall outside the target itself. This is what the theory says, and this is why in my text I mention that the choice of the Orkan to fire on targets in Zagreb was not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Whilst we're there, might I just ask you a question. It may appear to be overly simplistic, but on page 60 that first sentence: "The Serbian Krajina army units did not conduct an attack on the city of Zagreb." Now, my understanding is that there was an attack on the city of Zagreb. What is your scientific basis for reaching the finding in that sentence, to get me to understand what you meant? Are you talking about a general attack on Zagreb, as opposed to specific targets in Zagreb, and what the intention was? Or what is it? What is your scientific basis also for this finding? It may already be there, but please give it to me in what is the substance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was speaking about fire support, to go back to the attack itself, the units of the Serbian Army of the Krajina did not launch an attack on Zagreb. Their units did not move in the direction of Zagreb in order to attack it. All they did was carry out general fire support, and we said that general fire support implies artillery firing on enemy targets, and they were not firing at their units. It's not firing on enemy units; it's firing on enemy targets which at a later point could act against the units of the Army of Serb Krajina. In other words, there was no organised attack by brigades or corps on Zagreb. Only artillery fire was used against Zagreb, only the Orkan, and this is general fire support. In order to attack the city of Zagreb, which is a very large town, one would have had to have huge numbers of units moving towards Zagreb. As far as I know, this was not done. All that was done was this general artillery fire with the Orkan on targets in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you've put it very, very clearly. I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, we are now dealing with the use of artillery in a populated area. You answered Their Honours' questions referring to the use of artillery in a populated area. So I will ask you about chapter 5.2 entitled "selecting weapons and targets." Chapter 5.2 says that: "Multiple rocket launchers are used to carry out powerful, sudden, and rapid strikes against targets of exceptional importance and large dimensions and that as such they are unsuitable for firing on targets in populated areas." You give an example in the form of a table where you show the firing distance and you compare the effects. You have H203 millimetres. Is that a gun?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And underneath you have SRL, is that the Orkan system?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the Orkan system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you compare the effects of these two systems, you first make a comparison when firing at 15.000 metres, where the dispersion is marked as 27 in the first weapon and 38 in the second. So the dispersion is higher in the case of the Orkan than it is in the case of the Howitzer. Then you go on to talk about the dispersion in the range of 16.000 metres, and again in the case of a Howitzer it's higher than in the case of the Orkan. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You then go on to speak of ranges of 20.000, 30.000, and 40.000 kilometres, and you give the Orkan dispersion, but you don't provide any dispersions for the Howitzer. Is this because the Howitzer cannot be fired at such long ranges?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The range of the Howitzer is 16.000 metres or a little bit more, which is why I was able to give these figures for the Howitzer only up to 16.000 metres. Beyond that range the Howitzer is not effective. It cannot be fired at that range, so I could not draw the comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's just what I was about to ask. And in connection with the title of this chapter, "selecting weapons and targets," the fact that the Howitzer does not have this range, and apart from the Orkan this was the highest calibre weapon that the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina had, does this mean that at a distance of 30.000 or 40.000 metres only the Orkan can be used? And is this what actually defined the selection of the artillery piece to be used?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When selecting an artillery piece to be used, the type of target is one of the elements to be taken into consideration; and the second element to be taken into consideration is the range. If the range exceeds 30 kilometres, then I have to use the artillery piece which can be fired at that range. This of course in relation to the weapons that the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina had means that only the Orkan system could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In answering the Prosecutor's question you explained that the Orkan was fired from a distance of 47 to 50 kilometres. And my question in relation to this is the following: Did the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina have any other artillery system which it could have used in order to fire on Zagreb, in view of the range, apart from the Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer to this, although in one of the documents I read there is also mention of a Luna ground-to-ground projectile system, but I don't know whether at that point in time, the 2nd and 3rd of May, the Serbian Army of the Krajina still had this ground-to-ground Luna rocket system at its disposal and whether it could have been used. I assume that the Orkan was used because at that point in time, in that location, the Serbian Army of the Krajina did not have the Luna at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the range of the Luna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can recall, the ground-to-ground Luna rocket system - and I was present only once when it was fired - has a range of approximately 70 kilometres. There are several types, so I can only say approximately what types of the Luna system were within the Serbian Army of Krajina's equipment. I don't know whether there were any such systems in the vicinity of Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May and whether they could have been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it multi-barrelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The ground-to-ground Luna rocket system is a rocket. It's not multi-barrelled. It's a single rocket which is launched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask a question right there, please. I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. But could that Luna have been used in those circumstances by the RSK without injury to the civilian population under the same circumstances at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very hard to say because I'm not an expert on ground-to-ground Luna rocket systems. What I can say is that in the artillery training centre where I taught the artillery rules of firing, we did not even mention firing the Luna rocket system. Therefore, any discussion on the dispersion pattern and so on would be very difficult now without the appropriate tables. It would be hard for me to give you relevant information. Therefore, I feel it's better for me to refrain from commenting on the efficacy of that system or its dispersion pattern when fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, now that we mentioned the Luna rocket system, that's a ballistic rocket of tactical range, a 70-kilometre range. It's a single rocket on a launching vehicle. It's launched under an angle. Its diameter is 60 to 70 centimetres. It's length is six to seven centimetres. It has a very powerful warhead. Would the use of such a system in Zagreb have represented a disaster?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions about that. When firing on a populated area - I have only a few questions to go - we have considered the use of a multi-barrelled system on a populated area. This is a terrible topic, but we are talking about war. Is there a single fire weapon, even a pistol, an automatic rifle, a hand-grenade, a machine-gun, is there any weapon that can be used in such a way that the civilian population is completely safe in a populated area?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a populated area, any use of weapons is dangerous for the civilian population as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When discussing projectiles which are guided and those which are not guided, the Orkan rocket system is not guided?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: One of the logical questions is: Would the use of guided rocket projectiles have produced the number of victims. So I will ask you the following. The NATO pact fired 1.500 cruise rockets on the -- on Yugoslavia, and there were 2.500 dead and many wounded. Does the use of such guided missiles exclude civilian victims?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje. Let's move on to the next chapter, the use of the Orkan on the 2nd and 3rd of May by the Army of Serbian Krajina. Under point 6.1, you say that the directive or ordered Gvozd, G-v-o-z-d, determined that the artillery system Orkan should be moved to a firing position in the broader area around Korenica. And you state that it is the aim of the Orkan system deployed in the Korenica region pursuant to the Gvozd directive had the special assignment of preventing enemy reserves from being brought in an organised fashion along the axis. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in the directive on the deployment of the Serb Army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does it also say that bringing in the Orkan system from one area to another, from one locality to another, for example into the area or region of Korenica, was -- that it should be ready to carry out strikes against sectors and axes in accordance with developments on the ground, depending on how the situation developed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you go on to speak of an order of the Serb Republic of Krajina dated the 2nd of March, 1995, and this is on page 74 of the B/C/S text, in which you quote under one of the items that: "The Orkan unit is part of the 7th Mixed Artillery Regiment and its use can only be approved by the commander of the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina," that is Mr. Celeketic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says in the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, furthermore, when speaking about the quantity of ammunition for multiple-barrelled rocket launchers, you say that: "The Orkan system had a total of 160 rockets, of which 40 pieces in the 7th Corps and 76 pieces in the 75th Anti-Armour Battalion." Does that mean that the total arsenal of rockets intended for this multiple-barrelled rocket launcher was 116 rockets in total?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to quote an order to raise combat readiness issued by the Main Staff, and it is dated the 1st of May, 1995. And you quote the order. Under number 1: "The Orkan squad must be ready to be deployed pursuant to an order of the command of the Main Staff." Second, that: "The Orkan's system from Knin should be transferred to Vojnic where it will deploy personnel and materiel." Under number 3 you quote the order as saying that: "The command of the 21st Corps will select an officer to receive personnel and materiel and take in the units." And then in point 4 you say who was in command of the system, and you quote the order and say: "The commander of the Orkan squad will be deployed at the command post of the 21st Corps ready to receive tasks from the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Serbian Krajina or Colonel Djilas." And General-Lieutenant Celeketic signed this order.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any dilemma whatever that the -- this is commanded by the commander of the Main Staff or Colonel Djilas? Is there any room for doubt on the basis of this order?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We can conclude on the basis of this order that the deployment of Orkan, the decision to deploy Orkan is taken by the commander of the Main Staff of the SVK or Colonel Djilas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje. Now, this is the order of the 1st of May, 1995, whereas Orkan went into action on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995. Did you have any other document or evidence which would indicate that somebody else, apart from these individuals, commanded the system? For example, Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the documents that I received and I had and quoted in my document show that the competence and authority for the deployment of Orkan lay with the commander of the Main Staff or Colonel Djilas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the direct [as interpreted] on the deployment of the Army of SVK on the -- on e-court, please. And the number of the directive is 188710. I don't know if I've got the number of the document right. May I just take a moment to check, please. Thank you. I'm doing my best to have this directive placed on the monitor on the deployment of the SVK. It is the directive on Gvozd. We've already used it during the examination-in-chief. Perhaps the Prosecution can help me out to save wasting time. I'd be very grateful to them if they could. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think the 65 ter number, Your Honours, is 1887. I don't have the exhibit number handy, but I'll check and if this is not enough I'll check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic said 188710.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the number provided by the Prosecutor is correct. I have the 65 ter number as being 1887. Here it is, directive on the deployment or use of the Serb Army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, do you recognise the directive of February 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the first page of the directive?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the upper right-hand corner it says: "State secret." The code name is Gvozd. And the official name is: "Directive on the use of the Serb Army of Krajina." Is that right, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you acquainted and familiar with this directive?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read the directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this directive elaborate the variations of the aggression of the Croatian army on the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says when it was written, although I don't see the reason for the 2nd and 3rd of May, this directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have on the monitor page 4 of the directive, and the digits at the top are 815, number 815 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Point 3 on page 815, there's a title: "The probable way to solve the aggression and axes of action." And below that we have a text saying that: "An aggression by the Republic of Croatia against the Republic of Serbian Krajina would probably take three stages and that the third stage would be an attack operation with radical -- with a radical goal." Is that right, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, just a second. We are lost. When you say "815," I see 8.950, and then where do we go from there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was referring to page 4 in the B/C/S, which in the upper right-hand corner has the digits 02119815, so I was referring to the identification of that page in the B/C/S text. At this point in time I regret to say that I don't know what the equivalent page in English is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe it's page 5 in English. The ERN number at the top ends in 8954.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe that's the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, 89 -- what is the heading you are dealing with, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is point 3, probable or possible ways in which an aggression can be carried out and the axis of operation. That's the text I had in mind. So this is a directive which provides for the possibility of further action in the development of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have found it. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you found the page? And may we go ahead two pages -- or rather, back to point 2 which refers to "our forces." This is the directive of the Serb Army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So "our forces," Mr. Poje, does that refer to the forces of the Army of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that it was signed by the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina, then it does refer to -- when it says "our forces," it refers to the forces of the Serbian Army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje. Now, just before the break one short question in this regard. In the first chapter, at the end of the first paragraph, where it says "our forces," it says: "Bearing in mind the aforementioned, the Serbian Army of Krajina has the following assignment: To prevent sudden aggression by persistently defending the features and preventing penetration in depth and to liberate occupied territory." Now, does this text refer to the possible tasks of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina if there is an aggression against them by the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Should an attack be launched on the area of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, then that's what the army would have to do in case of an aggression of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this is a good time to break. It's 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and we'll come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, your time is up. How long are you still likely to be with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not much longer, half an hour at the outside. A little patience, with the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try and be as efficient as possible. That would be the outside limit. May I go ahead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We left off discussing the 1995 directive. And in that directive may we take a look at chapter 5, which is titled "the tasks of the units." In B/C/S the page number is 02119820. It's page 9. We have the page in front of us -- or rather, before that page comes up on the screens, may we have the whole page? Referring to unit tasks 5.1 mentions the 11th Corps; then the -- 5.2 is the 18th Corps, the 39th Corps, the 21st Corps; 5.5 is the 15th Corps; and 5.6 of this directive refers to the 7th Corps. Now, with respect to those corps, is it correct, Mr. Poje, that these were all corps of the Serbian Army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the directive says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje. Now, for each of these corps, the ones that I enumerated, in each of these points, it says, for example, that the 11th Corps, in the case of an aggression, will set up a decisive defence in Baranja in order to prevent the breakthrough of Ustasha forces. For the 18th Corps it says that under all conditions it will set up a resolute defence to prevent the breakthrough of Croatian forces. For the 39th Corps, once again, resolute defence and prevention of the advance of enemy forces. The same is for the 21st, the 15th, and the 7th Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina. When it comes to the 7th Corps it says: "Decisive action to prevent the breakthrough along the axis of Benkovac, Knin and Sibenik, Drnis to Knin, and from Sinj and Vrljika towards Knin," along those axes. Now, in connection with all the provisions of this directive, is it absolutely clear that this is a directive which looks at the defence plans of the Republic of Srpska Krajina and its army in case of an aggression by the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say first and foremost the following. I'd like to tell the Court this first. The subject of my expert report was not to deal with military action from February, when the directive was written, up until May. What my task and assignment was, that on the basis of the information I was given, I should calculate the dispersion pattern during the shelling of Zagreb. So I didn't deal with tactics, operation tactics, or the deployment of the units themselves on either side, one or the other side. That was not the task I was given or the assignment I was given. I have read through all the documents of course, I have all the documents, but it was my task and assignment that on the basis of the information I had at my disposal to calculate the dispersion pattern during the shelling of the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995, to determine the dispersion pattern, and to see what area is covered by that military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje --

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: But let me answer your question. We're talking about defence, yes, organisation of defence of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't insist on that topic. And the last question linked to directive. 5.8 relates to artillery, and point 2 of that chapter, you quoted the directives that Orkan be deployed along the firing positions in the region of Korenica. That means if there were an aggression that is where Orkan would be placed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, preparations for defence. The directive represents preparations for the defence of the -- of Srpska Krajina by the army of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also quote an order which shows us that on the 1st of May, 1995, that system, Orkan, the Orkan system, was moved into the area of responsibility of the 21st Corps and that that is where it was positioned at the point you showed us on the map. Is that right, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to that order, Orkan was moved from the locality it was in to a new locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would you say that it was correct that the deployment of Orkan in a new location on the 1st of May came at the time of the Croatian aggression under -- on the zone protected by the United Nations under the term Bljesak, or Operation Flash, Croatian Operation Flash? Did you read paragraph 80 of the indictment where it says that the Flash Operation was on May the 1st?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the penultimate page or the last page of your report you state under 6.2.2: "Impact dispersion during the firing on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995." That's the title of 6.2.2, that from the documents, on the basis of the document, which relates to the attack on the town of Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May and the records of the 30th of May on-the-spot investigation, you -- on-site investigation report, you established that the casualties did not include soldiers or military equipment, and you conclude on that basis that the target was not military facilities or military units. Now, in relation to that assertion I want to ask you: Is it only basis of that police report, what was established on-site and the on-site investigation report, that you're able to conclude what the target of the firing was?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I didn't have any other information, and we have already come to the conclusion that I did not dispose of the targets, I didn't know what the targets were, the targets that had been planned, I had to use the report that I was given about the casualties of the shelling of Zagreb. And on that basis I was able to conclude - and I'm sure you studied that document, too - in that document no mention is made of military casualties, that is soldiers or military equipment or military units. The report only contains civilian casualties and damages done to civilian buildings, the infrastructure, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that answer of yours, does that mean that the documents that the Prosecution showed you make no mention of any military targets, the military targets that might have existed?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I supposed -- I assumed that there might have been military targets, but I didn't get any information specifically as to the targets that were being aimed at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'm just cutting you off, Mr. Poje, to save time, no other reason. So I do apologise for having to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have a look at Exhibit 95, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: 95 is a document, a Prosecution document, which has been produced during the trial and has been provided to the Defence, and it is a report on the security of the Main Staff of the SVK of the 2nd of May, 1995. On the first page -- and you have the document in front of you, can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 2 and 3 of this document, it says that in the Pakrac pocket 5 to 6.000 people --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: What was the verb there, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon hours of the 2nd of May an infantry artillery attack started from Vljestina [phoen] launched by Ustasha forces attacking Pakrac which made it difficult for people in the Pakrac pocket, especially children and elderly persons. So does that talk about the combat operations going on in part of Western Slavonia during Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does talk about Croatian forces operations against the Serb army of Krajina, although I don't see what that has to do with Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, we'll get to that in due course. Now, in the last paragraph on that same page it says that the Serbian army of Krajina shot down a MiG 21, and that was done by the 18th Corps of the SVK. I don't know whether you know in that connection that the pilot of that MiG plane was a very well-known JNA pilot, Rudolf Perisin, who during Croatia's secession fled to Austria in 1991 and here we have him back again in 1995 to launch rockets against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, although I didn't hear of a pilot who had fled to Austria, but I don't know who the pilot was or what he did after he fled to Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a look at page 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Milovancevic? You are being asked to please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I will bear that in mind. I speeded up a bit when you asked me how much time I needed, but I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 1, speaks of targets, and it says that at 10.30 hours artillery units of the SVK fired from Orkan and now the targets with mentioned, Banski Dvori, that is the presidential palace, the Ministry of Defence and the Pleso airport using eight rockets. In continuation it says: According to our sources, the Ministry of Defence in Krizancevo Street was hit and then the collateral damage is mentioned as well. In the next paragraph it says that according to Reuters that the building of the Main Staff was hit as well as the Hotel Esplanade was confirmed that that is what happened when the Orkan was used. And in this connection my next question to you, Mr. Poje, is this: The deployment of Orkan, targeting these military targets, that is to say Banski Dvori, the presidential palace, the Ministry of Defence, and Pleso airport, would that be aiming at targets which can be termed to be the targets for which Orkan was intended to act against, that is to say large, important military targets and facilities? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we said previously, because we're dealing with general fire support and the targets you mentioned Banski Dvori, which is the presidential palace, the Ministry of Defence, the General Staff of the Croatian army, the airport, and so on, are possible targets which you could target with the Orkan system. They fall in that category.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as military targets then in Zagreb, we have the presidential palace listed, the Ministry of Defence, Pleso airport, all of which were hit, can we say and conclude that these were operational or strategic goals even, and that as such those targets represented the target of this indirect artillery fire as provided by Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were the possible targets in line of the general fire support that Orkan was used for, a different weapon could have been used, but in this case it was indeed Orkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So these three targets that were enumerated, according to the rules of the artillery profession, are military targets are they not, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the third paragraph of this page, of this report, it says that there is reliable information that citizens of Zagreb are leaving the city in large numbers and are moving towards the Republic of Slovenia, which has closed its borders to fleeing civilians. And according to another assessment, as many as one-third of the citizens of Zagreb are moving outside the city. Another part here says that Tudjman, the president of the republic, left Zagreb in the afternoon and went to Brioni for unknown motives, and it is assessed that along with General Tudjman members of the Main Staff left, along with him. This effect of the Orkan system, is this the demoralising effect on the enemy that you spoke about when discussing the effects of Orkan activity, materiel, and demoralising activity?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether these things really happened. These are just assessments by a body or an organ after the attack on Zagreb, and I cannot say whether this actually happened or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you, Mr. Poje, to confirm that this was actually the case, but rather to comment whether in your understanding if this did happen, this would have been a result of the demoralising effect of using such an artillery system?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the methods of action. It's possible. It's possible for this to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is this demoralising effects on the general population or the president of the republic and members of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned movements of the civilian population, you mentioned movements of the leadership of Croatia, so the answer would be both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this document which I have shown to you, Mr. Poje, I have another question. Is the aim of every military operation, every combat operation, to protect territory and to protect the population in general from physical destruction by enemy fire? Can one say that?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Poje, was: Is the main point of every defensive fire, whoever carries it out, in whatever kind of fighting, in principle protection of territory, preventing the enemy from taking territory, and also preventing the slaughter of the population being defended, the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the person carrying out the attack has to take into account when firing on military targets that there will also be civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, that's clear to every layperson. I asked you something else. We are now speaking of general artillery support to the Serbian Army of the Krajina in the fight it is waging in Western Slavonia. This fight during Operation Flash, or any other operation, because my question is a general one, was defensive fighting have as its aim the protection of territory and the protection of one's own population?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the task of every army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poje. That was my question, that answers it. As the Office of the Prosecutor has not shown you a single document relating to military targets which may have been the targets for the Orkan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, your learned friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The documents that were provided to Lieutenant-Colonel Poje are mentioned at the beginning. And I can just name one, Exhibit 94 makes reference to a number of documents, so I think it's a mischaracterisation of the evidence to suggest that we've somehow neglected to give him a full range of documents identifying military targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is very brief, Your Honours. The expert said that he had not received a single document which would speak of any possible military targets. And my question had to do with the following. About two years ago we received such a document which was in the possession of the OTP, but the military expert has not received it. I will leave out the preamble to my question. I will withdraw my question and reformulate it in order to avoid wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your preambles are the ones that you have been warned against right through this trial, Mr. Milovancevic. Let me say to you that -- were you not in this court when Mr. Black showed the witness Exhibit 94 that he's talking about? I'm asking you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what exhibit this is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know either, but he tells you that it's a -- it's a document that talks about military targets. In any case, you should know what the documents are that the Defence -- the Prosecution showed the witness and what they identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has just stated that he did not see any such documents, and under Rule 94, as far as I understand, the Prosecutor stated that the expert listed the documents he used in his report. That has nothing to do with my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about Rule 94?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about Rule 94? I'm sorry, interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Referring to the rule mentioned by my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your learned friend has not mentioned any rule; your learned friend has mentioned an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the expert report is submitted under a certain rule of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I believe this is Rule 94. When the witness submits his report, the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Rule 94 deals with judicial notice, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the situation, Your Honour, which my learned friend had in mind just a moment ago, and I wanted to explain that my question had to do with the expert's statement that he did not receive from the Prosecutor a single document pointing to possible military targets. That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm saying to you, Mr. Milovancevic, your learned friend says he showed the witness Exhibit number 94 in which, amongst others, military targets were pointed out. Now, you -- and hence I asked you the question: Were you not in court at the time when that happened? And if you were in court and you were aware what is contained in Exhibit 94, you can just tell the witness that in fact you did receive these documents, you look at Exhibit 94 which the Prosecutor showed you, and you will see these documents -- these targets there. It's simple as all that without having to go into any argument with the witness. Anyway, your learned friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. I hope I didn't misspeak before. I didn't -- did not use Exhibit 94 in court, but it's one of the documents that is referred to in the report as one of the ones that was provided to him. It's a subtle distinction, but I don't want Your Honours to be under the impression that I was saying that we used Exhibit 94 in court, but rather it had been provided to the witness. While I'm on my feet, if I could, Your Honours, what the witness said on page 63 of the transcript today is that: "I didn't get any information specifically as to the targets that were being aimed at." What he's saying is he didn't know the intended targets. He's not said that he got no documents about the impacts. Quite the contrary. I believe he said that he did receive documentation about the impacts. I mentioned Exhibit 94 because it makes reference to Pleso airport, for instance, which is one of the suggested targets I believe that Mr. Milovancevic has mentioned. Perhaps more to the point, Exhibit 95, which we're looking at right now, is a document prepared by the SVK. This -- the documents that we've provided, that we thought relevant to this report were documents about the actual impact prepared by the UN or by the local authorities that dealt with the actual impacts on Zagreb, not about what the SVK had to say about its attacks, and I hope that explains why certain documents were provided. Obviously we didn't provide all the documents that we had relevant to this. We tried to provide the ones that seemed most important and most relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. First of all, Mr. Black has now explained that Exhibit 94 was not used in court. For that the Bench retracts what it had said about that. Secondly, he now also explains the kind of documents that he gave to the witness and that this document that you are talking about is a Defence document and not -- well, it's a document prepared by the SVK, not by the Prosecution. Having cleared that situation, what was your question, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked Your Honour's leave to rephrase my question, to put it anew, afresh, and to eliminate any suggestion of anything from my question. So I withdraw the question and I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do rephrase it. And maybe if you can eliminate all those prefixes every time you ask questions, that would be very helpful. 30 minutes is running out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Please can we have Exhibit D1D0011 on the monitor. Could we have it turned right way up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, this is a report from Sector West of the civilian UN police, and in the third -- it's dated the 2nd of May, 2005 [as interpreted], and in paragraph 3 it says that on the way to Novska many ugly signs and at least 50 dead bodies were observed on the road. These were both Serb soldiers and civilians. Many houses were destroyed by shelling." Does this report of the 2nd of May indicate to you that there was combat going on in Western Slavonia on the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next Defence document, please. It's 1D0012. Before we see this document, Your Honours, I wish to tender this document as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 782, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have before you a document dated the 4th of May, 1995, and it's a statement by Mr. Yasushi Akashi, the special envoy of the Secretary-General and the special representative. And it says that in spite of the agreement achieved on the 3rd of May about a complete secession of hostilities, Mr. Akashi expresses his deep concern because fighting is going on in several areas near Pakrac and so on and so forth. Does this report by Mr. Akashi of the 4th of May also indicate that there was ongoing fighting in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this report one can see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- there was still fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just say to the interpreters that when opposite counsel stands you've got to stop because he's actually objecting to what you are interpreting being said at all. Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I usually refrain from saying objection so as not to ask the interpreters to interpret two things at once, but maybe in the future it would be help if I do say objection right away. My objection, Your Honour, is I don't see how fighting on the 4th of May can have any relevance whatsoever to the shelling of Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May. It's simply irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's relevant for the -- it's irrelevant for the Prosecutor, but the attack is said -- on Western Slavonia is said to have taken place on the 1st of May, and Zagreb was shelled on the 2nd and 3rd of May. We, however, are trying to show that on the 4th, 5th, and 6th of May there was also fighting. So the claim of the Prosecution is completely incorrect. This is relevant for the Defence, and at the end of the proceedings we shall see which of these is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you are saying that -- you have said to the witness that whatever action was being taken in Zagreb was defensive action. Am I right in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if defensive action was taken on the 2nd and 3rd of May, how does that become defensive action against action that is taking place on the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the purpose of this question, if it said in the indictment when Operation Flash began and when it ended, we don't have this. So any conclusions drawn would be pre-empting things. These are facts which have to be established in these proceedings, and the Defence is attempting to do so. The expert is able, possibly, to assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The expert has been telling you all afternoon, too, that he doesn't see how activities in Slavonia -- Western Slavonia affect any action in Zagreb. He has told you this, and you have finished your 30 minutes of extra time that you asked for which were already extra on the extra that you had. And now you're asking questions that are not relevant to the indictment and you want the indulgence of the Court to give you time to ask questions that are not relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, I must remind you that the only three paragraphs dealing with Operation Flash and targeting Zagreb are paragraphs 50, 51, 52 I think, and 54. The entire operation, the disaster, is explained by the Prosecutor in four sentences, four lines. What is clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to the Defence -- excuse me, Your Honour, please let me finish my sentence -- is that any conclusion about what was happening on the ground is impossible at this time because the Court does not have the material on the basis of which it can establish what happened and what did not. Such a conclusion can be drawn only at the end of these proceedings. This witness has told us that he did not see any documents about military targets. I'm now trying to put questions to him and show him materials which will give him a basis for saying ultimately why and under what circumstances Zagreb was targeted. If the Defence is not able to do this with such an expert, then we have nothing to do here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The way the question is ruled out of order is irrelevant. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at exhibit number 112.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before this document comes up, sir, it's an UNCIVPOL and UNPROFOR document dated the 5th of May, 1995, showing that on the 4th of May, 1995, in the presence of Brigadier General Denar [phoen] and the Brigadier General Matalon and the entire UNPROFOR staff the artillery of the Croatian army hit the village of Gavrinci, especially civilian targets, at a point in time when all these high representatives of UNPROFOR had arrived in order to prevent precisely such a development. This is the document before us now, and what I have just told you is in the first and second paragraphs of this document, points 1, 2, and 4 -- or rather -- yes, they say that at 1355 heavy shelling with artillery, mortars, and automatic weapons is being aimed at the village of Gavrinci. All those present are under fire including the UNPROFOR generals. I won't show you any other documents, but my question in connection with this document is the following: Does this document, in your view as a military expert, show that on the 4th of May in the area of Western Slavonia there was still activity by the Croatian army against the army and population of the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I have the same objection to relevance, Your Honour. It seems to me that it's essentially the same question, that's it's about things that happened on the 4th of May. And for more background on this I note that some time ago in this trial Defence counsel, and the transcript cite is transcript 3822, Defence counsel explicitly said that Operation Flash is not a justification for Zagreb. Now, it seems that that's not the thrust of the cross-examination, but I don't -- given the law of this Tribunal on the doctrine of reprisal, specifically the Kupreskic trial judgement and even the Rule 61 proceedings in this case, I don't see how the allegation that this -- that what happened to Zagreb was retaliation or reprisal for Western Slavonia could possibly be justified and accepted. And consequently I don't see any relevance to these documents and the questions regarding Operation Flash. If it has some relevance that the Defence counsel could explain, that's fine, but I just don't see it at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're on your feet, Mr. Milovancevic. You want to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. An assessment or position that the shelling of Zagreb was retaliation or reprisal for Operation Flash is what the Prosecution has claimed, and I don't understand this position taken by the Prosecution. I feel a little sick over it. The only thing that was done was to avoid establishing the real facts. Now, should I link up this conduct with the situation that the Prosecution is trying to side-step his own responsibility for not accusing someone for this operation in Western Slavonia and the 168 dead that their witness Grujic spoke about and the expulsion 15.000 people that UNCIVPOL speaks about in their reports. So to claim something about something in advance and say that it is not relevant in advance and that it has nothing to do with the subject of discussion without giving the Defence an opportunity to ask questions linked to that subject matter is something that is completely unacceptable to me and represents a obstruction to the Defence's work and is doing harm and detriment to the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I will warn you now from the Bench that if the 168 people died somewhere, it is for this Tribunal to charge those people. And if you want to lay the fault at the feet of your learned friend for having not charged those people, you can do so but outside this court. In this court you are going to speak relevantly and relevantly to the charges that are before us and stop making disparaging remarks about your colleagues. And on that basis -- I beg your pardon, not on that basis but on the reason that this document is irrelevant, your question is ruled out of order and this document is ruled out of order. The objection is upheld. You may ask further questions that are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood Your Honour, asking any question which could be wrong, incorrect, or whatever about the cause and effect between the Operation Flash and the shelling of Zagreb on the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th of May is irrelevant. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic -- can I interrupt you, Mr. Milovancevic? I've ruled. Ask the next relevant question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, there is an UNCIVPOL report which says -- which talks about a total massacre of the Serb population which in refugee columns during Operation Flash which lasted on the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, and 6th of May, that the Serb population was massacred, killed, while they were in civilian vehicles, tractors, trucks, trying to save their own lives. During all that time there was fighting in the area. And my question is: Do you have any material on the basis of which you would be able to state your views about the military justification or lack of it of having general artillery fire support in the form of firing at military targets in Zagreb, such as the defence ministry, such as the presidential palace, such as the airport, and similar features?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not interested in military operations or in Operation Flash. My task was not to monitor and assess and analyse military operations during the material time of Operation Flash. I'll state this once again. What was my task is this: That on the basis of the information I was provided with to calculate the dispersion pattern of hits when the Orkan artillery system was used, and on the basis of that, to draw my conclusions, whether it was right and proper to target military facilities in Zagreb, given this high dispersion. That was my task, not to look at the general situation. I saw Operation Flash and followed Operation Flash on television, so that's all I can tell you. I can talk about what I write about in my report, and that means that on the basis of the information to draw a dispersion pattern. Now, if the Ministry of Defence building is 100 times 150 metres or 100 by 100 metres, that means that if the centre of the dispersion pattern passes through the central point of the ministerial building, it is not even 1 Vd, and on the basis of that I concluded that there was a high probability that when military targets or possible military targets are targeted, you mentioned some of them, that's what I meant, because there weren't any other military targets or military facilities in Zagreb. So when rocketing facilities of that kind, there would be civilian casualties. Let me repeat again. Yesterday I calculated the dispersion pattern for 50 kilometres, it is about four hectares in area, the surface area is four hectares. It's a vast surface area. And so you must have foreseen in advance that in addition to the damage caused to a military facility you would have civilian casualties as well. So what you're asking me about now, what happened, how it happened, the operations and the units I know nothing about that. Nothing about operations, nothing about units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milovancevic, no further irrelevant questions. That was an irrelevant question. You are going to ask relevant questions only. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that general artillery support was the action in Zagreb. To whom was this support given, which units and where were the units active -- working from?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And where was it operational?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can see, somewhere in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So it was general artillery support to the Serbian Army of Krajina which was functioning in Western Slavonia. Was that during Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I can't say. I don't know. As I say, I don't know anything about Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your answer will suffice, Mr. Poje. Thank you. I have one more question linked to the very beginning, and I asked you when you left in 1991 the army you were lieutenant-colonel, and I asked you how long you were going to be a lieutenant-colonel for. And you said, quite rightly, that this isn't a question that I should be asking you, Mr. Poje.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to, I can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm going to ask you a new question now, another question, and it is this: Do you think that had you stayed in the JNA that you would have been a general long ago, judging by your years of service, your experience, your professional duties as a teacher and trainer and the work you were doing?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no. So let's go back to your first question, the one you asked me first yesterday. As you know, I am head of the department for artillery in the centre for doctrine and development, and that is the highest position of that kind in the artillery, the highest artillery position in the Slovenian army, and you must be aware of the fact that the Slovenian army has 6.000 soldiers, professional soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: One more question. How old were you when you became a lieutenant-colonel in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became a lieutenant-colonel -- well, I don't know if it's relevant, but I became a lieutenant-colonel in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Poje, I have no further questions for you. That completes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have some questions and I'll try to go through them as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Firstly, Lieutenant-Colonel Poje, a couple times, I think yesterday and today, you were asked about the possible effect of the bomblets on buildings. Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Ordinarily, what kind of damage to a building would -- could you expect from one of these bomblets?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said that on impact the bomblets impacting on an obstacle, an explosion takes place. The fuse leads to explosion when the pellets or small balls are released in a circle of a diameter of, let's say, 10 metres approximately. The second part of the operation is the high explosive effect which means that this cumulative spray or beam that is caused through the explosive charge of a special shape pierces the obstacle, and what is created is a subpressure which affects the environment. In most cases, all these little balls or pellets which are released remain outside the obstacle, that is to say, when the bomblet hits or impacts a target or obstacle, they fly off and those pellets or little balls do not do the piercing of the obstacle themselves. They disperse in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you now a question about this television camera adjustment that you were asked about today. Do you remember those questions about the TV adjuster on the M87 Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every Orkan has a camera which records the active phase of the flight of the trajectory, of the rocket, and it has a computer which is automatic, and comparing two trajectories is able to launch the next projectile better with the deviations recorded by the camera and calculated by the computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How long is that active phase of the flight of the rocket?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The active phase of the flight of the rocket is 4.3 seconds, after which the motor, what we call a motor, is extinguished, ceases to work, and then from that time on the rocket flies just like any other projectile that has been released from another weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So does the television camera or in any other way does the M87 Orkan observe the impact points?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be clearer, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness not once mentioned a camera that records the effects of the rocket but just a camera that records the initial stages of the flight and trajectory and sends back information about how to correct the figures for the next rocket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, do you have any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't disagree with that, but I don't see the objection, Your Honour. I certainly didn't suggest that the witness had said anything. I don't think I've mischaracterised the evidence. I don't understand the objection, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is your objection, Mr. Milovancevic? What are you objecting to specifically? The fact that the witness did not mention a rocket that -- I beg your pardon, a camera that records the effects of the rocket?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question that the Prosecutor asked indicate -- says that allegedly the camera records and films the impact of the rocket, which is not what the witness said and that is why I am objecting. The expert explained in great detail what the camera actually does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's how I understood the question. It was a question: So does the television camera or in any other way does the M87 Orkan observe the impact points? The answer could be yes or no on that. I don't know what is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Your substantive point is that it's not arising out of the cross-examination that was given, having regard to the question itself? It is a very technical area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. That's right. We did not in the cross-examination make any mention about the camera recording or filming the place of the impact, the point of impact. The witness never mentioned that. He was speaking about something quite different. But in the question the Prosecutor has just asked there is a suggestion of that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could I respond, please, Your Honour. I certainly didn't mean to suggest the possibility. I was simply asking so that we can clarify this. And the reason, with respect, I do think it arises from the cross-examination. A number of questions were put about this TV adjuster, and the suggestion was made that the TV adjuster adjusts the firing of the rocket in a similar way as to what traditional adjustment of firing is by someone who is observing the impact points and can say: You're 50 metres too far to the left, or you're 20 metres too far to the right based on observation of impact. Those are not the same thing, as I understand it, and I wanted the witness to explain that so that it's clear. Because I think the cross-examination confused that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed. Ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Poje, the question was simply: Does the TV adjustment camera of the M87 Orkan, does that observe the impacts?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That camera which is on the Orkan is used to record the rocket once it is launched on its trajectory for 4.3 seconds, its active phase flight. This trajectory, the real trajectory, which the first rocket follows, is calculated with the pre-calculated trajectory so that the following, the next, rocket is launched with new initial elements which calculate this difference between the theoretical trajectory and the actual trajectory. So with the system of a television camera and recording from the Orkan, you don't see the effect, the impact, of the rocket projectile on the target. All you can see is the active phase of the flight immediately after the rocket has been launched, and that active phase lasts 4.3 seconds which is the time that the motor is working. And then you use an algorithm to calculate the trajectory, and then that trajectory is compared, the real trajectory is compared to the theoretical trajectory calculated by the computer on the basis of initial firing data. And if these two trajectories differ from each other, then the following rocket is launched with these adjusted values and corrected launching.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. I guess my primary question: Does this TV adjustment, does this eliminate the impact dispersion pattern that you talked about at length yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispersion pattern, regardless of the way observation is carried out or in which measurement is carried out, is what I calculated it to be yesterday. The parameters of this dispersion pattern are in the table -- in the firing tables, and we cannot influence it. In other words, independently of the method used to observe the rocket trajectory, even if we have secured observation of the target area, we cannot influence the dispersion area, because there is no mechanism by which the dispersion pattern can be immediately reduced. It can be introduced by more modern methods, collecting ballistic and meteorological data and so on and so forth, but the means that were used could in no way have reduced the dispersion pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you've made that quite clear. You were also asked a number of questions during the cross-examination about whether the Orkan may have been the only weapon available to the SVK with a sufficient range to reach Zagreb. Do you remember that line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the question. But I answered that at the time the Orkan was used to target Zagreb, I don't know whether at that time the Serb Army of the Krajina had other weapons available which they could have used against Zagreb. Certain documents I have seen do mention other weapons, but I assume that the organ could have been the only artillery piece in the area capable of reaching Zagreb. I don't know. I cannot say whether they had other means available.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I understand that. My question is really this: If firing the Orkan at Zagreb was inappropriate for all the reasons that you set forth in your report, does it somehow become appropriate simply because it's the only weapon with sufficient range?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what led the Main Staff and Supreme Command to use the Orkan. I can only assume that at that point in time the army, the Serbian Army of the Krajina, did not have other artillery pieces or weapons -- weapons systems in the area that they could have used against targets in Zagreb, which is probably why they decided to use this, but I can't say that for sure. Because it's a range of about 50 kilometres. And I think we've already said that the only other system that could have been used would have been the Luna system, the ground-to-ground missile. And I think that we concluded that the effect would also have been enormous. And, again, there would probably have been civilian victims, just as there were with the use of the Orkan. But I don't know whether those launchers were within range of Zagreb or not and whether they existed still at that point in time or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps if I put my question this way. Does your opinion about the appropriateness of the Orkan, is it changed at all by whether or not the Orkan was the only weapon available to the SVK at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, someone decided to use the Orkan to fire on targets in Zagreb. That person would have to be acquainted with the consequences. It is very easy to conclude what the consequences would be, just as I did yesterday. I sat down, I took a pencil and paper, and calculated the dispersion pattern. Possible military targets in Zagreb, such as the ones enumerated today, the General Staff, the presidential palace, the Supreme Command, or a communications centre, for example. These would all be relatively small facilities. I don't know what the size of the General Staff is, whether 100 by 100 metres or 100 by 150 metres. It was a building or a compound. The size of those buildings is smaller than the dispersion ellipsoid or ellipse. So it's easy to calculate, even a layperson could calculate, that when using the Orkan with this large dispersion pattern would certainly lead to civilian victims and that civilian facilities would also be targeted. I therefore asked myself whether it makes sense to use that weapon and cause so many casualties. I, however, was not the one to make that decision. The person who made that decision probably had reasons of his own when he made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You gave a detailed answer and I understand what you said, but perhaps you're just missing the narrow point of my question, which is the following. You've explained -- in fact, just now you've explained quite clearly why it is inappropriate to use the Orkan against Zagreb. Is that opinion about its inappropriateness, is it affected, is it changed, would it be changed if the Orkan were the only weapon available to them? I'm sorry to persist on this, but I just want you to answer that question for me, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that even if Orkan were the only system which it would be possible to use to target Zagreb, for the reasons I have just mentioned because of the high probability that a large part of the dispersion pattern would fall outside the target, I think it was inappropriate and made no sense to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I appreciate your patience. I have just one final question for you. Has anything that you -- that has been put to you by the Defence counsel on cross-examination or any other thing that you've heard in the discussion over the last two days, does any of that change your opinion as stated in your expert report regarding the appropriateness -- in fact, the inappropriateness of firing on Zagreb with the M87 Orkan?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the two days I have been testifying here, and based on the task I was given to calculate the dispersion pattern on the basis of data and to establish the effects on facilities and military facilities in Zagreb, I remain convinced that firing the Orkan on targets in Zagreb should not have been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because according to the report I studied, and I see today how many victims there were, I think it made no sense to use it against Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Lieutenant Poje. I also have no questions for you. Let me thank you formally on behalf of the Chamber for coming to testify. This brings us to the end of your testimony. You are excused now. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess this will be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned. We'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.
